description: We are Team MINDCORE, a group of students passionate about space, technology, and innovation. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to turn our ideas into a creative and interactive space game while learning, exploring, and solving real world challenges together.
summary:
Mindcore is an interactive web-based Space Mission Design and Simulation platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It allows users to design spacecraft, select components, manage a virtual budget, explore launch vehicles and orbits, and simulate missions.

The platform includes an Earth Intelligence Center that integrates Sentinel-2 Level-2A satellite imagery through Microsoft Planetary Computer. It also uses Meteomatics for weather information and OpenStreetMap Nominatim for geographical location data. Users can explore satellite observations, weather conditions, mission simulations, and generated reports in one place.

Mindcore is built using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python, FastAPI, and JSON datasets. It is deployed on Vercel, with source code hosted on GitHub.

The project's goal is to make space mission planning more accessible and educational through interactive learning and practical experimentation. All simulations and risk assessments are illustrative, not certified engineering predictions.

Live Project: https://mindcore-space-mission-simulator.vercel.app/

Source Code: https://github.com/puneetk0204/mindcore-space-mission-simulator
details:
Mindcore: Space Mission Simulator

Mindcore is a web-based Space Mission Design and Simulation platform developed to make space mission planning more interactive, accessible, and educational. It allows users to explore the process of designing a space mission through a single workspace.

Users can start by selecting a mission type, configuring a spacecraft using available components, choosing a launch vehicle and target orbit, and running an educational mission simulation. The platform includes a virtual credit system that helps users understand how different component choices affect a mission's simulated budget. Users can also review mission reports to understand the outcomes of their decisions.

An important part of Mindcore is its Earth Intelligence section, which connects the platform with real-world data services. It uses Sentinel-2 Level-2A satellite imagery through Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC, providing imagery previews and information such as acquisition date and cloud cover. It also integrates Meteomatics weather data for parameters such as temperature, rainfall, and wind speed, along with OpenStreetMap Nominatim for location-based information.

The main benefit of Mindcore is that it brings several stages of mission planning into one accessible web application. Instead of only reading about spacecraft and mission design, users can interact with components, compare choices, explore orbital options, and understand how different decisions influence a simulated mission.

The intended impact is to encourage interest in space science, satellite technology, and space mission design, especially among students and beginners. It aims to provide a practical learning environment where users can explore complex concepts through experimentation.

The project was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the frontend, Python with FastAPI for the backend, and JSON-based datasets for spacecraft components, launch vehicles, orbits, and satellites. External services include Microsoft Planetary Computer, Meteomatics, and OpenStreetMap Nominatim. The application is deployed on Vercel, with its source code maintained on GitHub.

The creative aspect of Mindcore is the combination of a spacecraft builder, virtual mission budget, mission simulation, reporting system, and Earth observation data in one platform. It connects the learning experience with real satellite and weather data rather than limiting the project to a static presentation or a basic simulation.

During development, our team considered accessibility, ease of use, the relationship between component selection and mission costs, the availability of external data, and the importance of presenting mission information clearly. We also considered deployment and accessibility so that users can explore the project through a public website without installing additional software.

Mindcore is designed as an educational simulation. Its simulated results are illustrative and should not be treated as certified engineering calculations or real-world launch-safety recommendations.
